scores.position: STAY on Next.js/TypeScript and pay down the confirmed debt with a scoped, shippable refactor.
scores.strengths: Its checkable claims check out, which is rarer than it sounds. I reproduced the eslint finding exactly: `npx eslint middleware.ts modules themes` returns 4 no-restricted-properties errors at middleware.ts:23:22, 34:8, 74:5 and 74:46 while `pnpm lint` runs `next lint` (package.json:14) and never visits those paths, and .eslintrc.json's overrides never exempted them. Coverage matches to the decimal (coverage/coverage-summary.json: 37.42 lines, 62.56 functions, 79.91 branches). 49 verdicts across the four verify-*.json files are all real=true and exactly 26 carry matters_next_12_months=true. 14 runtime dependencies, 9 modules, 40 pages, 60 API routes, lib/catalogue-access.ts at 88 lines, lib/video/provider.ts at 151 - all confirmed. The strategic core is right for the situation: the company is pre-revenue with 6 orgs and 5 catalogues and `grep -rli razorpay` over the whole tree returns nothing, so the binding constraint is that there is no way to take money, and the only position that leaves 8 of the next 12 months free to build one is this one. Every slice ships independently; the cost of being wrong is one sprint. Its two cheapest items (R2 the live_at fix, R6a the lint fix) are a day each and remove the two findings that actually reach a guest. And the R1 proposal - a driver-conformance suite plus `supabase gen types typescript` against the ~20 hand-written column maps - buys most of the compile-time guarantee the rival positions spend 9 to 18 months on, for about 10 days.
scores.weaknesses: Three real defects. First, it undercounts severity: it says 'exactly two are high severity and both are the same liveOnly root cause', but three verdicts carry corrected_severity 'high' and the third (verify-deployability: every alert path runs through a GitHub Actions scheduler that .github/workflows/notify-drain.yml:14-15 says disables itself after 60 days of repo inactivity) is a different root cause. R5 does address it, so the plan is sound and only the framing is self-serving. Second, R3 overpromises. lib/catalogue-cache.ts:13-17 is not describing a correctable mistake - whether a guest may see a passcode-gated catalogue depends on that guest's cookie, so those routes cannot be cached across guests at all. Removing the unconditional cookies() call in lib/guest-locale.ts:22-23 and the awaited searchParams gets non-passcode catalogues to static; it does not get 'the guest page' there, and 6 days is optimistic for a change that must not break Publish visibility. Third and most telling: it never mentions hiring. The bus factor is one author plus an agent across 179 commits, and 'Next.js App Router with RSC plus a hand-rolled 103-method repository seam' is a materially narrower hiring pool in India than Java or Go. That is the one argument the losing positions make that this document has no answer to, and it simply omits it. It also leaves the largest untested surface - 13,326 lines of components at 17% coverage - to R7, which it marks optional and last.

scores.position: Port the backend to Go - one binary in two roles (api, worker) against the same Postgres, keeping React and Bunny, as a strangler.
scores.strengths: The best-engineered plan of the three and the most honest advocate. Its diagnosis is genuinely sharper than STAY's: the runtime is scattered across Vercel crons, GitHub Actions, PostgREST-over-HTTP and per-process memory, and several findings are artefacts of that scattering rather than of the code. Verified: vercel.json registers exactly two crons, the other four ride notify-drain.yml, and the 60-day self-disable is stated in the workflow's own header. Its refusal to decompose into services is correct - Publish touches catalogues, titles, photos, credits and notifications in one commit, and any boundary you draw cuts a transaction. Its insistence on keeping Next for the guest tree rather than going to Vite is right for the 1.5s-on-4G target. Two items are worth more than the position that contains them: the shadow-read in month 1 (run both drivers, return the old answer, log divergence) is precisely how the live_at bug would have surfaced before it shipped, and the month-2 stop point is an intellectually honest pre-commitment most rewrite proposals never make. It also corrects STAY on a real point - the guest page is not ISR-cached today - with the right citation (lib/catalogue-cache.ts:13-16).
scores.weaknesses: Its own thesis defeats it. If 80% of the value is banked at month 2 for 1.5 of 13 engineer-months, then 11.5 months buy 20%, and the document says so. Worse, it never prices the alternative that buys that same 80%: Vercel Pro is about ₹1,900/month and six entries in vercel.json, which is an afternoon, not 1.5 engineer-months. Its evidence is stale by one commit - it cites HEAD as 96fb305 when HEAD is 7730633 - though the listTitles claim it rests on is still true and I verified it (lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1390-1392 filters `.eq('published',true).eq('status','ready')` with no live_at predicate, against lib/db/memory-repository.ts:746-757 which gates on liveAt and explains at length why). 'A sync.Map plus LISTEN/NOTIFY is ~200 lines and strictly better than revalidateTag' is wrong on 'strictly': lib/catalogue-cache.ts:30-37 documents that the data cache survives deploys on disk and describes the exact bug that caused; a sync.Map does not, and the costs section concedes this while the architecture section does not. It scores worst of the three on the grants criterion by not engaging with it at all. And the 13-engineer-month estimate is priced at a velocity (179 commits in five weeks, one author plus an agent) that the document itself admits is weaker on a port, where the correctness criterion is 'matches undocumented behaviour' and the agent cannot check it.

scores.position: Port the backend to Java 21 / Spring Boot behind the existing React front end, as a strangler over four slices.
scores.strengths: The most intellectually honest document of the three, and it loses partly because of it. It is the only position that researched the grants criterion instead of asserting it: the SISFS ISMC scoring (market need, feasibility, potential impact, novelty/IP, team strength, fund-utilisation) and the eligibility gates (DPIIT recognition, incorporation within 2 years, ≥51% Indian promoter shareholding, ≤₹10 lakh prior government support) are confirmed against the primary sources in factcheck.json, and its conclusion - backend language appears nowhere in any of them, and eleven months of porting delays the paying customer that does count - is correct and argues against itself. Its hiring argument is the single strongest point any position makes that the winner does not address. Its measurements of the slice everyone under-scopes are the most precise in the set and I confirmed them: 26 of 40 page.tsx files read the repository inside a server component, and zero pages carry 'use client'. Its SESSION_SECRET finding is real and unaddressed by either rival - the secret is read by lib/auth.ts, lib/crypto.ts, lib/video/fake.ts and all six app/api/cron/* routes with no rotation path. Its pre-stated abandon trigger ('if slice 1 has not reached production by month five, stop') is the kind of commitment the winner's plan lacks. And its infra number is the only one that budgets log and metric retention, of which the repo currently has none.
scores.weaknesses: Its opening argument is factually dead. It claims lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1625-1631 'takes no options parameter at all' and that 'every photograph is visible to guests the instant the upload finishes, before Publish, in production, right now'. At HEAD the method signature is `listPhotosForCatalogue(catalogueId: string, options?: { liveOnly?: boolean })` and line 1642 applies `.not('live_at','is',null)`, committed as 7730633 at 11:27 on 16 Sept - five minutes before this document was written. The titles half is still live, so a defect remains, but the document's most urgent sentence is not true. Its component counts are wrong in both terms (it says 59 of 70 carry 'use client'; components/ holds 75 files and 64 carry it). The 18-engineer-month figure is not built up from its own slices, which total roughly 12-13, and its risk section concedes 'the honest range is 14 to 22'. Its central decision rule - 'this becomes correct the day a second engineer is hired' - is contradicted by its own costs section, which says the minimum viable team after the port is a Spring person AND a React person: the port raises the hiring bar it exists to lower. It damages the best idea in the codebase by its own admission, splitting the one-folder module contract (modules/billboard/index.ts: meta, schema, Guest, Editor, defaults, consumes and advise in 70 lines, held by tests/unit/registry.test.ts) across two languages with codegen between them. And at ₹23,300/month all-in it roughly doubles infrastructure for a pre-revenue product with no payment code.

winner: STAY on Next.js/TypeScript and pay down the confirmed debt with a scoped, shippable refactor. Do not rewrite in Go or Java.
rationale:
I have run a rewrite that failed, and the failure was never technical - it was that the rewrite was correct about the code and wrong about the calendar. That is exactly the shape here, and both rival advocates say so in their own documents. Go concedes the port 'is worth roughly 1.5 engineer-months of itself' and that the remaining 11.5 are 'a bet that a pre-revenue product with 6 orgs and 5 catalogues should spend two-thirds of a year not shipping'. Java concedes 'nobody should do this at 6 orgs and 5 catalogues pre-revenue'. When both prosecution witnesses testify for the defence, the verdict is not close.

The decisive fact is not in any of the three documents' architecture sections. `grep -rli razorpay` across the repository returns nothing; the plans table has zero rows and no reader; renewal is manual. A company that cannot take money has one problem, and it is not which language answers the HTTP request. Time-to-revenue carries weight 3 and it is where the three positions separate most: STAY leaves roughly eight of the next twelve months for commerce work, Go leaves none for eight months, Java leaves none for eleven and needs a second engineer who does not exist to hit even that.

On 12-month delivery risk (weight 3), the asymmetry is in the cost of being wrong. STAY's downside is one wasted sprint and a codebase with 26 fewer confirmed defects - which, as its own triggers section notes, makes the port case strictly stronger later. Java's downside is month eleven arriving with a half-strangled system, no Razorpay, and a hire that did not happen; Java names this as 'the plan's premise' and hedges it with nothing.

Maintainability at 3 years (weight 2) is the only criterion the ports win, and they win it narrowly rather than decisively. Go is right that TypeScript's structural typing is what let a driver implementation drop an options parameter and still typecheck, and right that one implementation tested against the real engine makes that class impossible rather than unlikely. But the same guarantee is buyable inside TypeScript for about ten days - a conformance suite executed against both drivers plus generated Supabase types over the ~20 hand-written column maps - and STAY prices it correctly. Paying nine to eighteen months for a guarantee available in ten days is the definition of a rewrite that looks rational from inside the code and absurd from inside the bank account.

Hiring (weight 1) is the one place the winner is genuinely exposed and simply silent. Java's case is real: the bus factor is one, and the Next App Router / RSC / hand-rolled-repository combination is a narrower Indian hiring pool than Spring. But weight 1 is weight 1, and Java's own costs section undoes the argument by conceding the post-port minimum team is two specialists rather than one generalist.

Grants (weight 1) is settled by the primary sources rather than by argument. DPIIT recognition tests entity type, age and turnover; SISFS scores eight criteria set by the incubator. Backend language appears in none of them, and a milestone-based grant is disbursed against proof-of-concept and product-trial milestones that an internal port cannot produce. Java deserves credit for establishing this and then reporting that it damns its own position.

One caution about the winner, because it should not be adopted uncritically. STAY's evidence is the most rigorous of the three - I reproduced its eslint finding exactly, and its coverage, line, dependency and finding counts are all accurate - but it is also the most self-flattering in framing. It reports two high-severity findings where three exist, its R3 caching claim is achievable only for catalogues without a passcode, and it plans least for the largest untested surface in the repository. Adopt the plan; do not adopt its account of how good the codebase is.
graft_from_losers: From Go, the shadow-read, run before the conformance suite rather than instead of it. Call both drivers on every read in a staging environment, return the Supabase answer, and log every divergence. This is the single cheapest thing in any of the three documents and it is exactly how the live_at bug would have surfaced before a guest saw it. It also tests STAY's own diagnosis - if fewer than about three real divergences turn up, the two-driver design is healthier than the reviews suggest and R1 can be scoped down.

From Go, the ordering principle: put the ops floor first because it is the item with the largest value-to-risk ratio, not because it is the most urgent bug. STAY's R5 already does this; make it explicit that it is the same 80%-of-the-value step Go pays 1.5 engineer-months for, bought instead with Vercel Pro (~₹1,900/month) and six entries in vercel.json. If that migration stalls for any reason, Go's worker - one long-lived process owning all six jobs plus the notification drain behind a Postgres advisory lock - is the correct fallback and touches no guest path.

From Go, generate the field-to-column maps rather than merely type-check them. STAY's `supabase gen types typescript` makes the ~20 hand-written maps in lib/db/supabase-repository.ts compile-checked against the schema; Go's sqlc point is stronger - a map that is generated from the column cannot drift from it at all. Generate where the shape permits and type-check only where it does not.

From Go, log the custom-domain cost explicitly. middleware.ts:100 states the constraint ('the slug is unknown until the database is consulted, which middleware must not do') and app/d/[host]/ is the whole parallel route tree that exists to work around it. That is a named architectural tax, and an edge-readable host→slug map would retire it without a language change. It belongs in NEXT.md as a numbered item, not as a comment.

From Java, make the real-Postgres test the default posture rather than a CI-only job. STAY's own risk list identifies the CI-against-a-real-branch half as 'the half most likely to be dropped under time pressure'. A disposable Postgres container that runs on a laptop removes that pressure. This is the most important graft on the list, because it is the difference between the conformance suite existing and the conformance suite being honoured.

From Java, make the org-scoping rule a type obligation rather than a filesystem walk. STAY's R1 test greps 34 route files for five guard names against an allowlist; Java's ArchUnit insight is that the rule should fail the build structurally. In TypeScript the equivalent is a branded session type that every repository method touching org_id demands as a parameter - then a route that forgets the guard does not compile, which is what CLAUDE.md claims about lib/admin/session.ts and cannot currently enforce.

From Java, the SESSION_SECRET untangling. Verified: it is read by lib/auth.ts, lib/crypto.ts, lib/video/fake.ts and all six app/api/cron/* routes, with no documented rotation path. Neither STAY's R10 nor Go's plan mentions it. Add it to R10 alongside the CSP and the photo signing.

From Java, a stated abandon criterion with a date on it. STAY's sprint 'ends when the ten items are done', which is how a debt sprint becomes a permanent state - a risk STAY names and then does not bind. Borrow Java's form: if R2, R6a, R5 and R3 have not all landed by the end of week eight, stop the sprint, keep what shipped, and go build Razorpay.

From Java, the grants conclusion, adopted as an action rather than a finding: incorporate the Pvt Ltd inside the SISFS two-year window and get one paying customer. Confirmed against SISFS §3.1 and G.S.R. 108(E), neither of which asks what the backend is written in. Both actions outrank every technical item in all three documents and neither appears in the winner's plan.

From both losers, the hiring answer the winner owes. The bus factor is one across 179 commits. Inside TypeScript the mitigation is that the conformance suite becomes the executable specification of the Repository's 103 methods, and R9's documentation collapse becomes the onboarding path. Name this as a deliverable of R1 and R9 rather than leaving hiring unmentioned - it is the losing positions' best argument and silence is not a rebuttal.
disbelieved: STAY: 'lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1632-1641 and the untracked tests/unit/supabase-query-shape.test.ts, both uncommitted as of 16 Sept' and 'the working tree carries M lib/db/supabase-repository.ts'. False. `git status` is clean and `git log` shows commit 7730633, 'Guests saw unpublished photographs on the Supabase driver', dated Wed 16 Sep 11:27:48 2026 +0530 - before the document was written at 11:30. tests/unit/supabase-query-shape.test.ts is tracked. The substantive claim (found and fixed within a day) survives intact; the evidentiary detail it is dressed in does not.

STAY: 'Two are high severity and they are the same root cause' / 'Exactly two are high severity'. Undercounts. Three verdicts across verify-*.json carry corrected_severity 'high': the two liveOnly findings (verify-maintainability, verify-scalability) and one in verify-deployability - 'All alerting runs through a queue drained by a scheduler that disables itself after 60 days of repo inactivity' - which is a different root cause and is the finding both rival positions lead with. STAY's R5 fixes it, so the plan is not compromised, but the count is presented as a tally of the evidence and the evidence says three.

STAY: 'R3 (6 days) - Make the guest page actually cached ... the shape is right; the enforcement and the caching are not.' Overstated. lib/catalogue-cache.ts:13-17 is a design argument, not a confession: 'whether a guest may see this catalogue depends on their cookies, and a page cached across guests could not answer it'. Removing the unconditional cookies() in lib/guest-locale.ts:22-23 and the awaited searchParams gets non-passcode catalogues to static rendering; a passcode-gated catalogue cannot be cached across guests at all. Go's correction - not ISR today, and not fully reachable - is the more accurate reading, and 6 days for a change that must not break Publish visibility is thin.

STAY: 'The frontend is untouched ... and a port cannot improve on one.' True and beside the point. verify-maintainability rates 13,326 lines of components at 17% line coverage with no component test on the four largest files, including CreateWizard at 1,006 lines. The only item addressing it is R7, which STAY marks optional, last, and 'the first thing to cut'. The position that most protects the front end plans least for it.

Java: 'lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1625-1631 - listPhotosForCatalogue takes no options parameter at all ... Every photograph is guest-visible on upload, before Publish, in production, right now.' False at HEAD, and this is Java's opening and most urgent claim. The signature at :1625-1628 is `listPhotosForCatalogue(catalogueId: string, options?: { liveOnly?: boolean })` and :1642 applies `.not('live_at','is',null)` under a comment naming the 15 September review. Fixed in commit 7730633 five minutes before the document was written.

Java: '59 of 70 files in components/ carry use client'. Wrong in both terms - components/ holds 75 .ts/.tsx files and 64 carry the directive. Go's '64 of 70' has the right numerator. It changes no conclusion, but Java repeats these counts as its evidence of measurement discipline.

Java: '18 engineer-months'. Not built up from its own slices, which total roughly 12-13 (0.5 contract + ~1 staging + 3 jobs + 2 guest path + 3 admin routes + 2 server pages + decommission). Java's own risk section concedes 'the honest range is 14 to 22 engineer-months and the wide end is more likely than the narrow one', which is the correct statement and is not the number on the label.

Java: 'It becomes correct the day a second engineer is hired.' Disbelieved as a decision rule, and contradicted by Java's own costs section: 'the minimum viable team is a Go person and a React person, and the rare, expensive hire is the one who can do both'. A port that converts a one-generalist product into a two-specialist product has raised the hiring bar it was justified by lowering. A second engineer is a reason to write down what exists - which is R1 and R9 - not to double the language count.

Go: 'Still true in the working tree at HEAD 96fb305'. Stale by one commit; HEAD is 7730633. The underlying claim is nonetheless TRUE and I verified it: lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1390-1392 gates publishedOnly on `.eq('published', true).eq('status','ready')` with no live_at predicate, while lib/db/memory-repository.ts:746-757 gates on liveAt and explains at length why `published` alone was the wrong rule, and lib/catalogue-cache.ts:62 feeds that query straight into the guest bundle. The titles half of the highest-severity finding is live in production today and every position wants it fixed.

Go: 'about 80% of the port's value is banked here [month 2], for about 1.5 of its 13 engineer-months.' Believed as advice, disbelieved as a case for the position it appears in - if it is true, the remaining 11.5 months buy 20%. More importantly, Go never prices the alternative route to that same 80%: vercel.json registers exactly two crons because the account is on a plan that allows two, and notify-drain.yml's own header says 'when the account moves to Vercel Pro, delete this file and put the entry back in vercel.json; the route itself does not change either way'. That is about ₹1,900/month and an afternoon, against 1.5 engineer-months.

Go: 'a sync.Map keyed by catalogue slug ... is ~200 lines and it is strictly better than revalidateTag.' Disbelieved on 'strictly'. lib/catalogue-cache.ts:30-37 documents that Next's data cache outlives the process - on disk under .next/cache locally and across deployments on Vercel - and describes the real bug that property caused (D-32, a stale entry served after a deploy). A sync.Map is better on inspectability and worse on durability across restarts. Go's costs section concedes the disk-backed point; its architecture section asserts the opposite.

All three, on infrastructure: the headline figures are not like-for-like and should not be compared as written. STAY ₹11,800, Go ₹15,800, Java ₹23,300, all claimed as monthly all-in at 10 weddings with Bunny at ₹7,534 from cost.json. But Java budgets ₹1,900 for a load balancer where Go budgets ₹560 for the same component on a different vendor, and Java alone budgets ₹2,800 for log and metric retention, which the repository currently has none of and which the other two omit rather than avoid. Normalised, the port premium over STAY is roughly ₹4,000-11,000/month depending on vendor, not the spread the three documents imply - and at a pre-revenue run rate the absolute numbers matter less than the eight to eleven months of unbuilt commerce either port spends.

Java, believed and worth stating because it argues against its own document: 'We rewrote the backend in Java scores zero on all eight [SISFS criteria].' Confirmed against factcheck.json's checks on the primary sources - SISFS §3.1 (DPIIT recognition, incorporation not more than 2 years before application, ≥51% Indian promoter shareholding, ≤₹10 lakh prior government support) and §7.2 (ISMC weighted scoring on market need, feasibility, potential impact, novelty/IP, team strength, fund-utilisation), and G.S.R. 108(E) for the age and turnover caps. Backend language appears in none of them. This is the most useful sentence in any of the three documents on the grants criterion and it was written by the position it defeats.
